findings.title: Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
findings.body: The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This service runs many jobs besides annotation cleanup: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, stale short URLs, and stale query history, plus a filesystem scan of temp directories. All of these now run 10x more frequently, which increases database and filesystem load across every Grafana instance, and the change is not mentioned in the PR description (which is scoped to the annotation deadlock fix). Since the annotation cleanup itself is already batched and self-paced, this global cadence change does not appear necessary for the fix and should either be reverted or justified and called out explicitly.

findings.title: Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists
findings.body: The new cleanup paths in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags emit `r.log.Error(...)` for normal, successful progress (e.g. line 534 "Annotations to clean by time", plus lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are not errors; they fire on every cleanup batch, and each message includes the full `ids` slice and the raw SQL condition. With the default batch size (and especially with the new 1-minute cleanup cadence in cleanup.go), this will flood error-level logs and any error-based alerting/monitoring with noise, and with large configured batch sizes (e.g. 32767) each line logs tens of thousands of IDs. These should be Debug level and should not dump the full ID list (a count suffices).

findings.title: Placeholder-limit workaround only applied to SQLite, not MySQL/Postgres
findings.body: deleteByIDs special-cases SQLite's 999-parameter limit by inlining IDs into the DELETE statement, but for other dialects it always emits `len(ids)` placeholders. MySQL and Postgres both cap parameters at 65535 per statement; AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable, so setting it above 65535 on MySQL/Postgres makes the DELETE fail every cycle (cleanup silently broken until the config is fixed and the error noticed). Since the code already handles the same class of problem for SQLite, the limit check should be applied per dialect (or the batch size validated at startup) rather than only for SQLite.
